sections.title: What every contractor invoice actually needs to show
sections.body: A generic bill of sale will not work for construction or trade work. Your invoice must reflect the reality of the site. Start with the original contract sum, then clearly list the percentage of work completed to date. You must separate labour costs from building materials. If the client holds back a retention amount to cover potential defects, show it as its own deduction line so the invoice states both what was earned and what is payable now. Whether retention reduces the taxable value of the supply or is simply a withholding of payment is set by your own tax authority, so check that before you decide where the line sits relative to tax. Finally, always include your specific payment terms and bank details so the client knows exactly how to settle the account.

sections.title: Managing progress billing and variation orders
sections.body: Large jobs are rarely billed all at once. Contractors rely on progress billing, invoicing for completed stages of work at the end of each month. This keeps cash flowing to pay suppliers and crew. The biggest complication is a variation order. When a client asks for extra work or different materials, the contract sum changes. You must invoice a signed variation separately from the original contract value. Mixing them together makes it impossible to track the original agreement, leading to confusion and delayed payments when the quantity surveyor reviews your submission.
items: Bill monthly based on the percentage of completed work
Never mix variation orders with the original contract sum
Require a signature on all variations before invoicing
Keep material receipts organised to justify cost increases

sections.title: Deposits, payment terms, and chasing late clients
sections.body: Cash flow is the lifeblood of any contracting business. You must secure a deposit before buying materials or breaking ground. Clearly state your payment terms on every document, whether that is seven days or thirty days from the issue date. When a client misses a deadline, you need a system to follow up immediately. Send a polite payment reminder the day after the invoice becomes overdue. If you use a proper invoicing tool, you can track which clients have viewed your document and record partial payments as they arrive in your bank.

faqs.q: How do I invoice for a variation order?
faqs.a: You should list an approved variation order as a separate line item or generate a completely separate invoice for it. Do not alter the original contract sum on your main progress invoice. Keeping variations separate ensures the client can easily verify the extra charges against their signed approval forms.

faqs.q: What is retention in a contractor invoice?
faqs.a: Retention, or retainage, is a percentage of the payment held back by the client until the project is fully completed and inspected. It acts as a security deposit against defects. Your invoice must clearly show the gross amount earned, subtract the retention percentage, and display the net amount currently due.

faqs.q: Should I separate materials and labour on my invoice?
faqs.a: Yes, separating materials and labour makes your invoice much easier for the client to understand. It shows exactly where their money is going and prevents disputes over pricing. Transparency builds trust, especially when material costs fluctuate. Some clients also require this split for their own tax and accounting records.
